units.translation: Sic Porsonus for προσπίτνω [I fall upon] προσκυνώ [I worship]
Sic Elmsley for πρόσπλαστοι [approachable], as ἄπλατος [unapproachable] everywhere appears in manuscripts as ἄπλαστος [unapproachable].
For they are savage and not approachable to strangers

Προσπορπατός [pinned to] is a corruption of προσπαρτός [pinned to]. See προσπείρω [I pin].
the summoner of the Erinys, the attendant of murder
with attendants, who guard my image
Προσπορπατός [pinned to] is a corruption of προσπαρτός [pinned to]. See προσπείρω [I pin]
The poetic form ποτισαίνω [I fawn upon] is perhaps to be restored in the epodic song
which the scholiast explains by εὐφραίνει [it gladdens]

where ἄρκυας Ἄτα [the nets of Ruin] has been corrected from the scholiast, and σαίνουσα [fawning] has been changed by Hermann to ποτισαίνουσα [fawning upon], for which Seidler had conjectured φιλόφρων γὰρ παρασαίνει βροτὸν εἰς ἄρκυας Ἄτα [for kindly it fawns upon a mortal into the nets of Ruin], with the words τὸ πρῶτον παρά-γει [first it leads astray] removed, so that the whole epode runs in full ionic feet to the end and is not interrupted by the catalectic foot παράγει [it leads astray], which however sometimes happens in ionic metre and has happened several times in this very song. But since the phrase τὸ πρῶτον παράγει [first it leads astray] is most apt and Aeschylus has used the verb προσσαίνω [I fawn upon] elsewhere too, Hermann's conjecture seems more probable. Moreover, Ἄτας [of Ruin] should be written with Hartung. For the subject of the verb παράγει [it leads astray] is not Ἄτα [Ruin], but the deception of the gods, as the scholiast noted.
if any of these things fawns upon you
it would not be like the Argives to fawn upon a base man
for kindly fawning at first it leads a mortal into the nets
for kindly it fawns upon a mortal into the nets of Ruin
For the subject of the verb παράγει [it leads astray] is not Ἄτα [Ruin], but the deception of the gods, as the scholiast noted
appointed to the fifth, the Borraean gates
but this has been commanded to us
who is the surety to stand before the gates of Proetus?
thus Scaliger for δείγμα [fear]. i.e. situated near the midriff and as it were before the doors of the midriff, as Blomfield explains.
why does this fear, standing before my heart, ever fly, a portent of my prophetic heart?
by the favor of Artemis the protectress
I will set against them a protector of the gates
we have fenced the gates with trusty single-combat protectors
and I say to the protectors of the Cadmeans
to send forth as a defender
to send forth as a defender
where the scholiast says: the justice of kinship sends him into battle.
